chunks.text: # ai-model-advisor — README Source: github.com/AdeelAsghar11/ai-model-advisor --- # AI/ML Model Advisor Expert System **Overview** This is a rule-based Expert System designed to recommend Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms based on user constraints. It utilizes a forward-chaining inference engine to deduce recommendations and a backward-chaining engine to explain the logic. [Image of expert system architecture diagram] **Features** * **Inference Engine:** Custom Python implementation using `SymPy` for boolean logic evaluation. * **Forward Chaining:** Derives new facts and recommendations from user inputs. * **Backward Chaining:** Explains *why* a specific model is recommended by tracing rules. * **Conflict Resolution:** Ranks recommendations based on rule specificity. * **Web Interface:** Lightweight Flask GUI for interaction. **Tech Stack** * **Language:** Python 3.x * **Web Framework:** Flask * **Logic Engine:** SymPy * **Data Storage:** JSON (Knowledge Base) **Installation** 1. **Clone the repository** ```bash git clone [https://github.com/yourusername/ai-model-advisor.git](https://github.com/yourusername/ai-model-advisor.git) cd ai-model-advisor ``` 2. **Install dependencies** ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` 3. **Verify Knowledge Base** Ensure `kb.json` is present in the root directory. **Usage** 1. **Run the application** ```bash python app_gui.py ``` 2. **Access the Dashboard** Open your browser and navigate to: `http://127.0.0.1:5000/` 3. **Get Recommendations** * Select your task (Classification, Regression, etc.). * Define constraints (Dataset size, Interpretability, etc.). * Click "Get Recommendation". **API Endpoints** * `POST /api/query`: Returns recommendations in JSON format. * `POST /api/backward`: Returns explanation traces for specific goals. **Project Structure** * `app_gui.py`: Main Flask application and inference logic. * `kb.json`: Stores the rules (Antecedents and Consequents).

chunks.text: # BSL-Hand_Gesture_Recognition — README Source: github.com/AdeelAsghar11/BSL-Hand_Gesture_Recognition --- # 🤟 BSL Hand Gesture Recognition System A deep learning system that classifies **British Sign Language (BSL)** hand gestures with **95.74% accuracy** across 34 classes — numbers (0–10) and alphabet (excluding H, J, Y). 🌐 **Live Demo:** [bsl-handgesturerecognition.streamlit.app](https://bsl-handgesturerecognition-rhu9sdhz9v9pzvxufdw2w7.streamlit.app) --- ## 📌 Overview | Detail | Info | |---|---| | Dataset | 34,000 images · 34 classes · 1,000 per class | | Model | MobileNetV2 (Transfer Learning + Fine-tuning) | | Accuracy | 95.74% | | F1-Score | 95.78% | | Deployment | Streamlit Web App | --- ## 🗂️ Dataset **BSL Hand Gesture Dataset** by Eren Tatepe 📦 [Kaggle Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/drmabroukaabuhmida/bsl-dataset-credits-to-eren-tatepe) - 34,000 images across 34 BSL gesture classes - Numbers: Zero (0) to Ten (10) - Alphabet: A–Z excluding H, J, Y - Perfectly balanced — 1,000 images per class --- ## 🔧 Pipeline ``` Raw Image │ ▼ CLAHE Normalisation (LAB L-channel, clipLimit=2.0) │ ▼ MediaPipe Hand Landmarker (21 keypoints) │ ▼ Bounding Box + 20% Padding → Crop │ ▼ Resize to 224×224 → Normalise [0,1] │ ▼ MobileNetV2 → Softmax (34 classes) ``` --- ## 🧠 Model Architecture - **Base:** MobileNetV2 pre-trained on ImageNet (frozen in Phase 1) - **Head:** GlobalAveragePooling2D → BatchNorm → Dense(256) → Dropout(0.4) → Dense(128) → Dropout(0.3) → Dense(34, Softmax) - **Phase 1:** Train head only · Adam lr=1e-3 · 10 epochs · Best val acc: 82.87% - **Phase 2:** Unfreeze last 30 layers · Adam lr=1e-4 · 20 epochs · Best val acc: **95.74%** --- ## 📊 Results | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Accuracy | 95.74% | | Precision | 96.04% | | Recall | 95.74% | | F1-Score | 95.78% | | Classes ≥ 90% Recall | 30 / 34 | --- ## 🚀 Run Locally **1. chunks.text: # CIFAR-10 Object Classification: A Classical Machine Learning Approach ## Overview This repository implements a classical machine learning pipeline for object recognition on the CIFAR-10 dataset using Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) and Support Vector Machines (SVM)[cite: 8]. It achieves a test accuracy of 62.74% without relying on deep learning, offering a highly interpretable and lightweight alternative suitable for CPU-bound environments[cite: 9, 25, 129]. ## Dataset The CIFAR-10 dataset contains 60,000 color images at a 32x32 pixel resolution, distributed perfectly evenly across 10 object classes[cite: 14]. The extremely low resolution, combined with high intra-class variation and inter-class similarity, makes this a challenging computer vision task for manual feature engineering[cite: 18, 20, 22, 23]. ## Methodology & Feature Engineering Unlike deep learning models that automatically learn feature representations, this pipeline relies on explicit feature engineering designed to extract structural information while reducing dimensionality[cite: 55, 56]. * **Grayscale Conversion:** Reduces the 3,072 RGB pixel values to 1,024 values on a single channel, prioritizing structural shape over color[cite: 57, 58, 59]. * **HOG Feature Extraction:** Captures edge orientations and gradient directions, making the representation highly robust to illumination changes[cite: 27, 28, 29]. Configured with 9 orientation bins, 8x8 pixel cells, and 2x2 cell blocks, this step achieves a 9.48x dimensionality reduction (from 3,072 raw pixels to a 324-dimensional feature vector)[cite: 33, 61, 62, 69]. * **Feature Scaling:** A `StandardScaler` normalizes the extracted features to zero mean and unit variance to ensure specific dimensions do not unfairly dominate the SVM decision boundary[cite: 65, 66]. To prevent data leakage, the scaler is strictly fitted on the training data only[cite: 67]. ## Validation Strategy To ensure credible evaluation and avoid artificial performance inflation, the original 50,000 training images were subjected to an 80-20 stratified split[cite: 43, 44]. This yielded 40,000 training images and 10,000 validation images, maintaining an exact class balance[cite: 44, 45]. This validation set served as a safe environment for hyperparameter tuning, keeping the standard 10,000-image test set completely untouched until final evaluation[cite: 42, 48]. ## Model Selection & Optimization Several classical classifiers were evaluated on the validation set: * **Linear SVM:** 50.88% accuracy[cite: 72]. * **K-Nearest Neighbors (k=9):** 49.02% accuracy[cite: 77]. * **RBF Kernel SVM:** 61.82% accuracy[cite: 74]. The Radial Basis Function (RBF) SVM was selected for its ability to implicitly map features into a higher-dimensional space to capture non-linear patterns[cite: 75, 82]. Hyperparameters were optimized via a `GridSearchCV` with 3-fold cross-validation on a 10,000-image training subset[cite: 85, 92]. The optimal configuration was determined to be `C=10` and `gamma='auto'`[cite: 96]. ## Results & Insights The final pipeline achieved an overall accuracy of **62.74%** on the held-out test set[cite: 101]. The minimal gap of 0.92 percentage points between validation and test accuracy indicates excellent generalization with no overfitting[cite: 102]. ### Performance by Class Type * **Strengths:** The model excelled on structurally distinctive objects with rigid shapes[cite: 104]. Automobiles achieved the highest accuracy at 78.4%, followed by trucks (72.8%) and airplanes (71.2%)[cite: 105, 106]. * **Limitations:** The model struggled significantly with classes reliant on fine-grained texture[cite: 153]. Cats yielded the lowest accuracy at 43.6%[cite: 108]. HOG is primarily a shape descriptor and fails to differentiate classes separated mainly by fur texture or surface details that are lost at the 32x32 resolution[cite: 110, 158]. ## Engineering Trade-offs While Deep Learning (CNNs) can achieve >90% accuracy on

chunks.text: # GeoSimAI **GeoSimAI** is a machine learning framework for geospatial similarity analysis using Google Earth Engine annual satellite embeddings (DeepMind AlphaEarth Foundations). It enables users to select a reference location and automatically discover, rank, and visualize environmentally and geophysically similar locations within a defined study region without relying on hand-engineered vegetation or surface indices. --- ## Guidelines & Configuration - [Agent Guidelines (AGENTS.md)](AGENTS.md) — Core directives and architecture conventions. --- ## Quick Start (Preview) ### Prerequisites - Python 3.10+ - A Google Cloud Project with the Google Earth Engine API enabled (Community tier recommended) ### Setup ```bash # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/<username>/GeoSimAI.git cd GeoSimAI # Create and activate virtual environment python -m venv venv .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 # On Windows # source venv/bin/activate # On Linux/macOS # Install dependencies (once requirements.txt is populated) pip install -r requirements.txt # Authenticate Earth Engine (local development) earthengine authenticate ``` ### Running the Application ```bash python run.py ``` Open your browser and navigate to `http://127.0.0.1:5000` to interact with the map interface. ### Selecting a Search Area Use **Draw AOI** in the Similarity panel, then click two opposite corners on the map. The selected city or small regional area is used for both similarity search and clustering. Pick a reference point inside that AOI, then run the analysis. AOIs larger than 2,500 km² are rejected to protect Earth Engine Community quota.

The problem we landed on: people scroll reels and social media every day, and every so often something genuinely useful appears — a recipe, a tip, an idea worth remembering. The instinct is to save it to look at later. But on almost every app, saved items become a graveyard. Either the save is never revisited at all, or by the time it is, it is buried under a thousand other saved items with no structure, no way to search, and no way to tell what any of them were about without opening each one. That was the whole problem statement: save is easy, retrieval is broken. ## The Solution: Sortd Sortd is an AI-powered content capture platform that automatically extracts, transcribes, categorizes, and makes searchable any content a user saves, closing the gap between saving something and actually being able to find it again. ### How it works 1. User captures a screenshot, link, or video (Instagram Reel, YouTube video) 2. Gemini Vision performs OCR and visual analysis on screenshots 3. Groq Whisper transcribes audio from video content 4. Content is automatically categorized and tagged 5. Everything becomes searchable through a unified interface ### Technical stack - Gemini 1.5 Flash — screenshot OCR and vision analysis - Groq Whisper — audio transcription for video content - React — frontend - Node.js / FastAPI — backend services - Supabase (PostgreSQL) — database and auth - PWA — installable progressive web app - Real-time SSE updates for live capture status ### Team collaboration Adeel and Muhammad Ismail worked collaboratively across every step of the build rather than splitting into strict frontend/backend roles — both contributed to the pipeline design, integration work, and problem-solving as the hackathon progressed. ## Challenges faced Time pressure was the defining challenge of the event. Wiring together multiple AI services (vision, transcription, categorization) into a working real-time pipeline within the hackathon window meant constant prioritization: getting the core capture-to-search loop working end-to-end mattered more than polishing any single piece. ## Judges' feedback The judges were specifically impressed that the team did not chase a big, sprawling problem. Choosing a small, relatable, everyday pain point — saved items nobody revisits — and solving it well stood out more than an ambitious idea solved poorly would have. ## What happened after Post-hackathon, Sortd was extended with RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) features using pgvector for semantic search over captured content, moving beyond simple keyword search to meaning-based retrieval across everything a user has saved. The project was also presented at HITEC University's Pitch Perfect competition, where it secured 2nd place.

chunks.text: # HITEC Mega Code War — 1st Place (AI Model Training) & 2nd Place (Pitch Perfect) ## Event HITEC Mega Code War, HITEC University, 2026 Two competitions entered on the same event. --- ## Competition 1: AI Model Training — 1st Place ### The challenge A classic machine learning problem: given a dataset, build the most accurate model possible within the competition's time and resource constraints. The dataset was highly imbalanced, which meant accuracy alone would have been a misleading target — the real work was in handling the imbalance correctly before model performance could be trusted. ### Approach Multiple models were trained and compared rather than committing early to a single algorithm, letting the data decide which approach performed best. Because the dataset was highly imbalanced, relevant techniques for handling class imbalance were applied before and during training rather than treating it as an afterthought. Alongside the modeling work, the code itself was kept clearly commented throughout — not just for readability, but because in a judged competition, evaluators reviewing the code benefit directly from being able to follow the reasoning behind each step without needing it explained verbally. ### Result 1st place — highest model accuracy among competing teams, achieved within the imposed speed and resource limits. ### Key learnings Comments in the code matter more in a competition setting than they might in a personal project — they are doing real work in helping evaluators judge the quality of the approach, not just the output. A well-reasoned, well-documented process reads as more credible than a black-box result, even when the result itself is strong. --- ## Competition 2: Pitch Perfect — 2nd Place ### What was pitched Presented the Sortd project (the same AI content capture platform that won HACKDATA V1) to a panel of 4 experienced judges, covering the product concept, architecture, and technical design decisions. ### Format 20+ teams competed. Each team presented their idea or prototype live in front of the judging panel. ### Result 2nd place. The judges responded well to both the product and the confidence of the delivery. ### Judges' feedback The panel loved the pitch and the confidence behind it. Their one substantive suggestion was to run pilot studies related to the project — validating the problem and solution with real users beyond the hackathon-built prototype. --- ## Overall takeaway Between the two competitions, the main lesson was less about the modeling or the build and more about communication: learning how to talk about a product, frame a problem clearly, and pitch with confidence in front of an experienced panel. That skill carried forward into how later hackathons and presentations were approached.

Could you provide the company name?" } ``` ### `GET /chat/{thread_id}/history` Retrieve conversation history for a thread. ### `GET /health` Liveness check. --- ## Key Features ### Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) via LangGraph `interrupt()` When the Clarity Agent detects an ambiguous query (no company name), it calls LangGraph's `interrupt()` primitive. This suspends the entire graph at that exact point. The API detects the suspension by inspecting `graph.get_state(config).tasks[0].interrupts` and returns a `clarification_needed` status to the frontend. When the user answers, the frontend sends the same `thread_id` again, the API detects the pending interrupt, and resumes the graph with `Command(resume=user_answer)`. The Clarity Agent continues from where it left off, injecting the user's answer as the resolved query. ### Multi-Turn Conversation LangGraph's `MemorySaver` checkpointer persists the full `ResearchState` between API calls. The `messages` field uses the `add_messages` reducer, so every message is appended rather than replaced. This means follow-up questions like *"What about their competitors?"* have access to the full prior exchange as context. ### Conditional Routing Three routing functions implement the branching logic as Python functions passed to `add_conditional_edges`. LangGraph evaluates these at runtime and dispatches to the appropriate next node. The Validator-to-Research loop is bounded by `research_attempts` to prevent infinite loops. --- ## AI Prompts Used & Reasoning ### Prompt Design Philosophy All agent prompts follow the same structure: 1. **Role declaration** — e.g. *"You are the Clarity Agent in a multi-agent business research system."* *Reason:* Role-priming improves instruction-following and reduces hallucination. 2. **Crisp task definition** — Single-purpose per agent, not multi-tasking. *Reason:* Reduces confusion and makes outputs more predictable. 3. **Explicit output format** — Every prompt specifies valid JSON only. *Reason:* Eliminates markdown fences, prose preambles, and parsing failures. A `_parse_llm_json()` helper strips any stray fences defensively. 4. **Calibration anchors** — The Research and Validator prompts include labelled score ranges. *Reason:* LLMs tend to inflate confidence scores without anchoring. Explicit rubrics produce honest assessments. 5. **Conversation history** — Every prompt receives the last 6–10 messages as context. *Reason:* Enables follow-up resolution (e.g. "their CEO" → resolved to the company from prior turn). ### Clarity Agent Prompt Instructs GPT-4o to return `clarity_status`, an optional `resolved_company`, and a `clarification_request`. The prompt explicitly tells the model that follow-up messages (e.g. "What about their CEO?") referencing a company established in history should be marked **clear**. This avoids over-triggering the interrupt on legitimate follow-ups. ### Research Agent Prompt Instructs GPT-4o to synthesise raw Tavily results into structured JSON with a `confidence_score` and `confidence_reasoning`. The scoring rubric (0–2 / 3–4 / 5–6 / 7–8 / 9–10) was designed after testing found that without it, the model consistently returned scores of 7–8 regardless of data quality. The rubric distributes scores more accurately. ### Validator Agent Prompt A second, independent assessment pass. The scoring rubric (0–2 / 3–4 / 5–6 / 7–8 / 9–10) was designed after testing found that without it, the model consistently returned scores of 7–8 regardless of data quality. The rubric distributes scores more accurately. ### Validator Agent Prompt A second, independent assessment pass. The model is told explicitly to ignore the Research Agent's own confidence score and evaluate the text on its own merits. The SUFFICIENT/INSUFFICIENT criteria include a "2-year freshness" rule, which catches cases where Tavily returns old filings or Wikipedia summaries. ### Synthesis Agent Prompt Instructs the model to write in professional-but-conversational markdown with an executive summary, logical sections, and key takeaways. The prompt conditionally adds a follow-up instruction if `len(messages) > 2`, so follow-up responses acknowledge continuity naturally rather than starting from scratch. --- ## Dependencies | Package | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `langgraph` | Graph orchestration, state management, interrupt/resume | | `langchain-openai` | OpenAI GPT-4o integration | | `langchain-community` | Tavily search tool wrapper | | `tavily-python` | Live web search | | `fastapi` | REST API server | | `uvicorn` | ASGI server | | `python-dotenv` | Environment variable management | --- ## Design Decisions - **GPT-4o at temperature=0** — Deterministic outputs are critical for JSON parsing and routing consistency. Creativity is handled by the Synthesis Agent prompt design, not temperature. - **MemorySaver (in-memory checkpointer)** — Appropriate for a demo/internship project. Production deployment should use `SqliteSaver` or `PostgresSaver` for persistence across restarts. - **3-search cap per Research run** — Balances comprehensiveness against latency. Empirically, 3 targeted queries cover company overview, financials, and news adequately for most queries. - **Confidence threshold of 6** — Below 6, data is likely incomplete enough that an independent validation pass adds value. Above 6, the cost (latency + tokens) of validation outweighs the marginal benefit. - **Max 3 research attempts** — Prevents runaway loops while giving the system two retry opportunities before falling back to best-effort synthesis.

OptiMill is a premium marketplace and orchestration engine for the manufacturing industry. It moves beyond simple directory listings by providing deep technical insights into 3D designs, allowing clients to understand the manufacturability of their parts before they even contact a supplier. ### What does it do? Configure `.env.local` with `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` and Supabase keys. 4. `npm run dev` ## 👥 The Team The OptiMill project is developed by a dedicated team of engineers focused on high-precision manufacturing workflows: - **Project Lead**: System Architecture & Core Logic - **UI/UX Designer**: Frontend Engineering & HCI Optimization - **Backend Engineer**: API Development & Geometric Analysis - **DevOps Engineer**: Database Security (RLS) & Infrastructure --- *OptiMill: Precision in Every Pixel, Perfection in Every Part.*

chunks.text: # SynthLab SynthLab is a local-first synthetic data studio for creating fictional, schema-driven datasets. A Python generation engine owns identifiers, categories, probabilities, numbers, dates, dependencies, and validation. A local Ollama model can assist with schema drafting and optional text enrichment, but it cannot overwrite structured row facts. The application combines a FastAPI backend, a React and TypeScript workspace, SQLite job metadata, and CSV/JSON export with quality and provenance reports. > SynthLab is designed for fictional data. It does not accept real row datasets and should not be used to reproduce identifiable people, private records, credentials, or financial-account data. ## What it provides - A versioned Pydantic dataset specification with strict generator/type compatibility. - Deterministic structured generation using seeded NumPy and SciPy samplers. - Random and fixed-proportion categorical generation. - Conditional categories, derived datetimes, nullability, uniqueness, and declarative constraints. - An AI Schema Builder that converts a short use-case description into a bounded field draft and compiles it into a strict specification in Python. - Optional local text enrichment through Ollama, with a local template fallback. - Background jobs with SQLite state, cancellation checkpoints, previews, reports, and manifests. - Spreadsheet-safe CSV and JSON exports. - Prompt, schema, and generated-text screening for prohibited fields and sensitive formats. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR UI[React workspace] --> API[FastAPI API] API --> POLICY[Prompt and schema policy] POLICY --> SPEC[Pydantic specification] SPEC --> ENGINE[Python generation engine] ENGINE --> TEXT[Template or local Ollama text adapter] TEXT --> SCREEN[Output screening and validation] SCREEN --> JOBS[SQLite jobs and artifacts] JOBS --> EXPORT[CSV, JSON, report, manifest] ``` The model boundary is intentionally narrow: 1. The Schema Builder screens the request before calling Ollama. 2. Ollama returns a bounded field-intent draft rather than executable code or a complete arbitrary configuration. 3. Python maps that draft to allow-listed field and generator types. 4. The compiled specification is screened and semantically validated again. 5. Job submission repeats the specification policy so the frontend cannot bypass it. 6. During row generation, the model may populate approved text fields only; structured facts remain fixed. ## Requirements - Python 3.10 or newer - Node.js and npm (tested with Node.js 24) - Ollama for AI schema generation and model-backed text enrichment Structured generation can use the built-in template adapter without Ollama. The AI Schema Builder itself requires the configured Ollama service and model. ## Quick start ### 1. Install the backend ```powershell python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 python -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Install the default model if it is not already available: ```powershell ollama pull qwen2.5:7b ``` If Ollama is not already running as a Windows service, start it in a separate terminal: ```powershell ollama serve ``` Start the API from the repository root: ```powershell python -m uvicorn backend.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 ``` The API is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`; interactive API documentation is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`. If the current Windows Python event-loop policy produces a socket error, use the selector-loop launch command: ```powershell python -c "import asyncio; asyncio.set_event_loop_policy(asyncio.WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy()); import uvicorn; uvicorn.run('backend.main:app', host='127.0.0.1', port=8000, loop='none')" ``` ### 2. Install and start the frontend In another terminal: ```powershell Set-Location frontend npm ci npm run dev ``` Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`. ### 3. Generate a dataset

A safe Schema Builder request looks like: ```text Create 500 fictional warehouse inventory records with synthetic item IDs, stock category, quantity, unit price, availability, and created timestamp. ``` Requests for real-source records, identity/contact fields, credentials, financial-account data, or guardrail bypasses are rejected before model inference. ## Configuration SynthLab reads configuration from environment variables. `.env.example` documents the available names and safe local defaults. | Variable | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | `SYNTHLAB_OLLAMA_BASE_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:11434` | Trusted backend Ollama endpoint | | `SYNTHLAB_DEFAULT_MODEL` | `qwen2.5:7b` | Local model used for schema and text generation | | `SYNTHLAB_SCHEMA_GENERATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `90` | Schema Builder request timeout | | `SYNTHLAB_DB_PATH` | `backend/data/synthlab.db` | SQLite job database | | `SYNTHLAB_ARTIFACTS_DIR` | `backend/data/artifacts` | Generated job artifacts | For example, to select another installed model in PowerShell: ```powershell $env:SYNTHLAB_DEFAULT_MODEL = "qwen2.5-coder:7b" ``` Model endpoints are backend configuration. They are not accepted from browser requests. ## Supported specification features | Field or rule | Supported behavior | | --- | --- | | Identifier | Deterministic prefix, index, padding, and uniqueness checks | | Category | Weighted random sampling or exact fixed-proportion allocation | | Conditional category | Distribution selected from a parent category | | Integer and decimal | Uniform or truncated-normal bounded sampling | | Boolean | Configurable true probability | | Datetime | UTC bounded sampling | | Derived datetime | Status-aware timestamp derived from existing fields | | Text | Template or local-model enrichment from approved row facts | | Constraints | Allow-listed declarative rules; no `eval` or executable validators | ## API overview | Endpoint | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `GET /api/health` | Storage and local inference health | | `GET /api/templates` | Available approved templates | | `GET /api/templates/{id}` | Complete template specification | | `POST /api/specs/generate` | Generate and validate a schema through local Ollama | | `POST /api/specs/validate` | Validate a specification and return diagnostics | | `POST /api/jobs` | Submit preview or full generation | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}` | Read job status and progress | | `POST /api/jobs/{id}/cancel` | Request cancellation | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/preview` | Read the bounded completed preview | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/report` | Read validation and quality results | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/manifest` | Read generation provenance | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/exports/{format}` | Download `csv` or `json` output | ## Safety and privacy boundaries SynthLab applies deterministic policy checks in addition to model instructions:

chunks.text: `POST /api/specs/validate` | Validate a specification and return diagnostics | | `POST /api/jobs` | Submit preview or full generation | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}` | Read job status and progress | | `POST /api/jobs/{id}/cancel` | Request cancellation | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/preview` | Read the bounded completed preview | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/report` | Read validation and quality results | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/manifest` | Read generation provenance | | `GET /api/jobs/{id}/exports/{format}` | Download `csv` or `json` output | ## Safety and privacy boundaries SynthLab applies deterministic policy checks in addition to model instructions: - Prompt screening occurs before the Schema Builder calls Ollama. - Generated and manually edited specifications are screened before use. - Job submission repeats the same schema policy. - Text output is screened for CNIC-like values, phone numbers, email addresses, payment-card formats, and other configured patterns. - Text retries preserve the original structured row skeleton. - CSV export neutralizes spreadsheet formula prefixes. - Services bind to loopback by default, and there is no cloud-model fallback. These controls reduce specific risks; they do not establish anonymity, differential privacy, legal compliance, or universal detection of sensitive information. Pattern-based screening can miss novel obfuscations and can conservatively reject harmless wording. Generated text may vary between model versions and devices. ## Verification Run the complete backend test suite and production frontend build: ```powershell powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\check.ps1 ``` Or run the components independently: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest -q tests Set-Location frontend npm run build ``` Automated tests avoid requiring live model output by using fake or template adapters. Real Ollama checks should be treated as explicit local integration tests because model output and runtime performance are probabilistic. ## Repository layout ```text backend/ api/ FastAPI routes specs/ Dataset contracts, templates, AI draft compiler, validation generation/ Samplers, generation engine, and text adapters policies/ Prompt, schema, and generated-text screening validation/ Dataset checks and quality summaries jobs/ SQLite state and job orchestration export/ CSV, JSON, report, and manifest writers frontend/ React, TypeScript, and Vite workspace tests/ Unit and API integration tests evals/ Reproducible evaluation runners examples/ Example specifications scripts/ Project verification commands ``` Generated databases, job artifacts, model files, frontend builds, local agent tooling, and evaluation results are intentionally excluded from version control.

Binary files are read as raw bytes, reshaped into a 2D pixel array, and classified by a ResNet50 model trained on the Malimg dataset across 25 malware families. The project demonstrates that malware classification is fundamentally a computer vision problem — different malware families produce visually distinct patterns when their bytes are rendered as images. ThreatLens exposes this entire pipeline through a professional security operations dashboard. --- ## How It Works ``` Binary File (.exe / .dll / .bin / .pdf / any) │ ▼ Read raw bytes as uint8 array │ ▼ Reshape into square 2D array (nearest square root of byte count) │ ▼ Convert to PIL Image → resize to 224×224 Convert to 3-channel RGB Normalize to float32 / 255.0 │ ▼ ResNet50 ONNX Inference │ ▼ Classification result + confidence scores across 25 malware families ``` Different malware families produce visually distinct patterns — Allaple worms look like structured noise, Lolyda trojans show repeating segment blocks, Yuner bots create striped gradient patterns. --- ## Architecture ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser │ │ React + Vite + Tailwind CSS │ │ Dark terminal aesthetic (localhost:5174) │ │ Sidebar nav: [S] Scanner [H] History [D] Dashboard │ └─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘ │ REST API calls (axios + JWT) ┌─────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐ │ Node.js API Gateway │ │ Express.js (localhost:4000) │ │ • JWT authentication & token signing │ │ • Multer file upload (any file type, 10MB max) │ │ • Request proxying to Django ML Engine │ └─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘ │ HTTP (multipart/form-data) ┌─────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐ │ Django ML Engine │ │ Django REST Framework (localhost:8001) │ │ • User registration & login │ │ • Byte-to-image preprocessing pipeline │ │ • ResNet50 ONNX inference │ │ • Scan storage & history via Django ORM │ │ • Dashboard statistics endpoint │ │ • SQLite database │ └─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐ │ ResNet50 ONNX Model (~90 MB) │ │ Trained on Malimg — 76.4% validation accuracy │ │ 25 malware families, 9,010 training images │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` --- ## Features - (2011) in *Malware Images: Visualization and Automatic Classification*.
